question: why can't we test an LLM app the same way we test normal software?
ideal_answer: Normal software is deterministic and rule-based, so the same input always gives the same output and you can assert one exact expected value. LLM applications are probabilistic, so the same input can produce different wordings, and most tasks have many acceptable answers instead of one exact string. That breaks exact-match testing, so LLM evaluation instead judges qualities of the output, usually against a golden dataset and often with an LLM as a judge.

question: what's the difference between model evals and application evals?
ideal_answer: Model evals test the capabilities of the raw LLM itself, independent of any product, and include benchmarks as well as custom model evals used to pick a model. Application evals test a system built around one or more LLMs, such as a RAG chatbot or an agent, evaluated end-to-end. In short, model evals judge the model, application evals judge the system you built.

question: what are the different methods to actually perform an eval?
ideal_answer: There are three broad methods. Programmatic (deterministic) evaluation uses code and fixed rules to check the output, which is cheap and reliable but only works when correctness can be expressed in code. LLM-as-a-judge uses a capable LLM to score outputs, which handles subjective or semantic judgments at scale. Human evaluation uses people to judge outputs, which is the most reliable for nuanced quality but the slowest and most expensive.

question: what does reference-based vs reference-free eval mean?
ideal_answer: A reference-based eval needs a ground-truth answer to compare against, a golden or expected output authored ahead of time, and scores the system by how close it comes to that reference. A reference-free eval needs no ground truth and instead judges an intrinsic property of the output, usually with an LLM as a judge. The test is simply whether the metric requires an expected answer.

question: offline eval vs online eval - what's the difference?
ideal_answer: Offline eval happens before deployment on a fixed golden dataset in a controlled setting; it is usually reference-based and is what you run during development to decide whether a version is good enough to ship. Online eval happens after deployment on live production traffic, works without ground-truth labels, and relies on real user interactions and signals like thumbs up/down, latency, and cost. Offline gates deployment; online monitors real behaviour.

question: what is drift and why does it matter after deployment?
ideal_answer: Drift is the gradual degradation of a deployed system's performance over time as real-world data or usage patterns move away from what the system was built and evaluated on. Users may start asking new kinds of questions or the knowledge base may go stale, so metrics slowly fall even though the code did not change. It matters because these failures appear silently in production, so you monitor metrics over time, set alerts when they drop, and feed failing cases back into your offline dataset.
